tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (nanoant/WebFrameworkBenchmark, not by Undertow authors) with public run scripts (time.sh, benchmarks/*/run.sh, configs) and raw wrk outputs in results/E5-1650v2-Ubuntu-14.04LTS/; the README table rows match those files (Undertow 616,547 is run 02 of 4, nginx 381,368 is run 01). Not A because compiler versions, the JVM and the resolved Undertow version are not stated and only some C builds carry flags; a small single-author suite (53 stars), so B is the ceiling.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Undertow: build.gradle requests io.undertow:undertow-core and undertow-servlet '1.0.0+' (dynamic, resolved at build time in late 2015), started with 'gradle run'; JVM and JVM flags not stated; default Undertow IO/worker thread counts. libmicrohttpd: helloworld.c built 'cc -O3' against the system libmicrohttpd (Ubuntu package, version not stated), MHD_USE_EPOLL_TURBO with a 12-thread pool. Crow: 'c++ -O3 -std=c++11' with boost_system, multithreaded(). Onion: cmake -GNinja with no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE plus a static libev (current Onion CMakeLists then uses -O2; the 2015 submodule was not checked). Kore: 'kore run', built with 'make NOTLS=1', 12 workers. nginx: the OpenResty-bundled nginx binary (/usr/local/openresty/nginx/sbin/nginx) with the echo module, conf/echo.conf worker_processes 4. Compiler versions not stated.
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon E5-1650 v2 @ 3.50GHz (results directory name), 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 14.04 LTS, Linux 3.16; wrk on the same host with 12 threads (common/threads.sh counts 'core id' lines) and 100 connections; time.sh does a separate 10 s warm-up call and four 20 s runs, and the README reports the best of the four.
corrections.claimed_speedup: 616,547 req/s (3.29 ms p99) vs Kore 572,782 (1.08x, derived from page data), libmicrohttpd 533,626 (1.16x), Onion 483,824 (1.27x), nginx with echo module 381,368 (1.62x), Crow 256,552 (2.40x). Each README row is the best of four 20 s wrk runs (Undertow's four runs: 607,522 to 616,547). Undertow's p99 (3.29 ms) is worse than libmicrohttpd's (1.28 ms) and Onion's (2.82 ms).
corrections.caveats: Benchmark is from November-December 2015 (last suite commit 22 Dec 2015) on Undertow 1.x resolved from a '1.0.0+' dynamic dependency, so it is far older than current Undertow, Kore, libmicrohttpd, Onion, Crow and nginx. Single-author suite (53 stars) re-running a TechEmpower-style plaintext hello-world on one 6-core/12-thread machine with the 12-thread wrk load generator on the same host. The nginx row is configuration-skewed: conf/echo.conf sets worker_processes 4 while Kore runs 12 workers, libmicrohttpd a 12-thread pool and Undertow defaults to one IO thread per logical CPU, so the 1.62x over nginx is not a like-for-like comparison; nginx was OpenResty's build answering 'Hello World!' as text/html with Date and Server headers stripped. Kore's MB/s (104.33) exceeds Undertow's (80.55) because it sends larger headers, so bytes per response differ across rows. JVM version and C/C++ compiler versions are not stated; Onion and Kore build flags are not given in the suite. Margins over the strongest C servers are small (1.08x Kore, 1.16x libmicrohttpd) and come from server architecture and thread configuration, not from Java codegen. The Undertow README itself carries no benchmark numbers.
corrections.why_faster: The suite gives no mechanism beyond 'most optimized'. From the scripts: Undertow's non-blocking XNIO handler sends a fixed string from its IO threads (one per logical CPU by default); the margins over Kore and libmicrohttpd are small and the nginx margin follows from nginx running 4 workers against 12 for the others, so the result reflects server design and configuration rather than the Java language or JIT.

notes: Numbers verified against the README and the raw wrk files. Shortcomings to record: 2015-era versions, load generator on the same host, nginx row crippled by worker_processes 4 (versus 12 threads/workers elsewhere), JVM and compiler versions unstated, small single-author suite, worse p99 than libmicrohttpd. Not a language-level win.

tier_reason: First-party Grafana screenshot (assets/bench.png) showing Aralez above nginx and Traefik in three 800-user batches; no table, no load-generator command, no nginx/Traefik versions or configs, so first-party with partial methodology is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Chart only, no table; approximate readings off assets/bench.png: HTTP/1.1 plain batch Aralez about 97k-108k req/s vs nginx peaks of about 72k-76k with repeated drops toward zero between three sub-runs, Traefik about 44k-58k; HTTP/2 over SSL batch Aralez about 71k-79k vs nginx about 40k-70k, Traefik about 33k-37k; mixed batch Aralez about 79k-88k vs nginx about 26k-76k, Traefik about 35k-44k. Peak-to-peak this is roughly 1.4x, 1.1x and 1.15x over nginx (derived from chart readings). README text separately says Aralez alone reaches 107k-110k req/s (glibc build) and 97k-100k (musl build) in its most intensive tests.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Current Cargo.toml (Aralez 0.94.4): release profile opt-level 3, lto true, codegen-units 1, panic abort; pingora 0.9 with the openssl feature (TLS through OpenSSL, as in nginx) and mimalloc. The Aralez version and binary used in the nginx/Traefik comparison are not stated; nginx and Traefik versions, build flags and configs are not stated.
corrections.caveats: Comparison numbers exist only as a Grafana screenshot (a panel from a dashboard filtered to host g01, cluster mouseflow-eu) with no table, so all values are approximate readings. The nginx series is unstable: within each batch it rises and collapses several times (down to about 26k-45k, and toward zero between sub-runs in the first batch) while Aralez and Traefik hold steady plateaus, which suggests nginx was restarted, re-run or misconfigured rather than measured at steady state; the README only says the proxies were 'Tuned as much as I could' without publishing the configs. The load generator, run duration and Aralez/nginx/Traefik versions are not stated. HTTPS crypto runs through OpenSSL on both Aralez (pingora openssl feature) and nginx, and Aralez links mimalloc, so the C code paths are shared. The README says results reflect 'synthetic performance under optimal conditions'; its text figures (129,777 req/s with oha, 107k-110k req/s) come from Aralez-only runs on a different CPU (Xeon E3-1270 v6) with zero-byte responses (oha 'Total data: 0 B') and are not comparable with the chart. HAProxy appears only in a feature table. Aralez is an application built on Pingora (cloudflare/pingora, already listed in wave 5); its own benchmark is separate from Pingora's Cloudflare blog claim.
corrections.why_faster: Not analysed in the README, which credits Pingora and tokio. Nothing in the evidence isolates a Rust-language effect: TLS is OpenSSL on both sides and the allocator is mimalloc (C); the visible gap may partly reflect nginx's unstable run in the chart.

notes: Chart readings in the record are roughly right but quote nginx peaks; nginx's trace is erratic with deep dips, so averaged gaps are larger and less trustworthy. Shortcomings to record: chart-only evidence, unpublished nginx/Traefik configs and versions, erratic nginx series, OpenSSL and mimalloc shared C paths, Aralez-only text numbers on different hardware with zero-byte bodies. Pingora (wave 5, https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora) is the engine underneath; I kept Aralez as a separate entry because the claim and measurement are its own, but the orchestrator may fold it.

tier_reason: The README table (179/194/200 vs 1209/1655/2146 ms) is first-party with no raw ab output (no Document Length, Failed or Non-2xx counts), and the repo's own benchmark/cblt setup (ievkz/cblt:0.1.2 with a Cbltfile for host 'example.com' only) would answer the documented 'ab ... http://127.0.0.1/logo.png' with 403 Forbidden under the 0.1.x host-matching code, so no valid measurement can be confirmed; the same week's earlier 5 MB run had cblt no faster than nginx.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README percentile table for 'ab -c 1000 -n 3000 http://127.0.0.1/logo.png' (23,911-byte file; ab reports ms): 50%: 179 vs nginx 1209 (6.75x lower, derived from page data); 75%: 194 vs 1655 (8.53x); 100%: 200 vs 2146 (10.73x). Feature list: '10 times faster than Nginx for small content under 100KB'. The table was added on 10 Nov 2024 (commit 3fb9fa5, version 0.1.5) and replaced an earlier 5 MB test (ab -c 100 -n 300, logo_huge.png) whose medians were cblt 1956 ms, nginx 1941 ms, Caddy 1768 ms.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile with lto = true (opt-level 3 by default); benchmark/cblt/Dockerfile runs the Docker image ievkz/cblt:0.1.2 (Alpine, cargo build --release) and overwrites its config with a Cbltfile for host 'example.com'; nginx is the nginx:latest Docker image with its default configuration; both run in Docker.
corrections.hardware: Not stated for the 23 KB table; the earlier README revision with the 5 MB test shows the runs were made from a Windows MINGW64 shell on a Lenovo machine with Docker containers.
corrections.caveats: Single first-party run of one 23 KB file with no raw ab output, so it cannot be checked that cblt actually returned the file: the repo's benchmark/cblt/Cbltfile (last changed in PR #4 'Highload', merged the same day the table appeared) defines only host 'example.com', and cblt 0.1.x returns 403 Forbidden when no '*' host exists and the Host header (here 127.0.0.1) does not match; only the root Cbltfile ('*:80', ./assets) would have served logo.png, and the README does not say which was used. The previous README benchmark (5 MB file, same week) showed cblt at parity with nginx (median 1956 vs 1941 ms) and slower than Caddy, and was removed rather than kept beside the new table. Medians above one second for nginx at 1000 concurrent connections for 3000 requests suggest connection queueing (listen-backlog overflow and SYN retransmission are a plausible cause, not verified) rather than per-request serving cost. Hardware, OS, Docker networking mode and the nginx config are not stated; the '10x faster for content under 100KB' headline rests on this one file. The benchmarked build was cblt 0.1.x (November 2024); the current crate is 0.6.2 (December 2024) and the last commit is June 2025.
corrections.why_faster: No mechanism given. cblt 0.1.x opens the file per request with tokio::fs and has no obvious advantage over nginx's sendfile path; the measured gap may come from a 403 response path or from connection-queue effects at -c 1000, not from Rust codegen.

notes: Downgraded C to D: no valid measurement can be confirmed (published harness config would serve 403 for the tested URL; no ab byte or non-2xx counts), and an earlier same-week test showed no win; not rejected because the 403 path is not proven (the root '*:80' config would have served the file). Shortcomings to record: possible 403 fast path, replaced parity result, single file, queueing-dominated latency at -c 1000, no hardware or nginx config, stale since June 2025. Metadata checked: MIT, 71 stars, 16 forks, crates.io 28,901 downloads, last commit 2025-06-04 (stale).
